revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Fingerprint Card Strips
revealWordProblem.text: The forensic lab has a 5-foot roll of fingerprint card paper. Each fingerprint card strip needs to be 1/3 of a foot long. How many complete fingerprint card strips can be cut from the roll? Explain what the division 5 ÷ 1/3 represents.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 5 ÷ 1/3 asks how many 1/3-foot strips fit into 5 feet. Each 1-foot section holds 3 thirds, so with 5 feet there are 5 × 3 = 15 strips. The lab can cut 15 complete fingerprint card strips from the roll.

conceptIntro.heading: What does it mean to divide by a fraction?
conceptIntro.intro: Dividing by a fraction asks one question: how many of that small piece fit inside the whole amount? For 3 ÷ 1/4, we ask how many 1/4-foot pieces fit into 3 feet.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Dividing Whole Numbers & Unit Fractions. Formula: a ÷ (1/b) = a × b | (1/b) ÷ a = 1 / (a × b). 1. Whole divided by unit fraction: How many fraction pieces fit into the whole (result is larger). 2. Unit fraction divided by whole: Split the fraction piece into smaller parts (result is smaller). 3. Multiply by the denominator of the unit fraction

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I want to cut a 3-foot strip of tape into 1/4-foot pieces. I ask: how many 1/4-foot pieces fit into 3 feet?
First I look at just 1 foot. How many 1/4-foot pieces fit in 1 foot? Four, because 4 fourths make one whole.
Now I have 3 feet. So I do 3 groups of 4: 3 × 4 = 12.
So 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12. There are 12 pieces. The answer is bigger than 3 because each piece is very small.

weDo.title: Let's do one together — a whole number divided by a fraction
lines: Let's try 2 ÷ 1/3. The question it asks is: how many 1/3-size pieces fit into 2 wholes?
How many thirds are in 1 whole? Three.
We have 2 wholes, so 2 × 3 = 6. That means 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6.
The answer is bigger than the 2 we started with, because each piece is smaller than one whole.

youDo.title: Your turn — now the other direction
lines: Now try 1/2 ÷ 4, a fraction divided by a whole number. This one asks: if half a pan of brownies is shared equally among 4 people, how much does each person get?
Draw the half, then cut it into 4 equal parts.
Each part is 1/8 of the whole pan, so 1/2 ÷ 4 = 1/8.
Notice the answer is SMALLER than the 1/2 you started with. Say why the two directions move opposite ways.

optional.stem: Agent Cole has 8 feet of evidence rope and cuts it into 1/3-foot pieces for tagging. What does 8 ÷ 1/3 mean?
choices: How many 1/3-foot pieces fit into 8 feet
8 feet shortened by 1/3 of a foot

optional.explanation: Dividing by 1/3 asks how many 1/3-foot pieces fit into 8 feet. Each foot holds 3 thirds, so 8 × 3 = 24 pieces.
choiceFeedback: You're thinking of multiplication. Does dividing by 1/3 ask 'how many parts' or 'what is part of the whole'?
Subtracting doesn't match the problem. Division by fractions asks 'how many pieces fit.'
That's describing the pieces, not what 8 ÷ 1/3 means. What question does the division ask?
optional.stemEs: El agente Cole tiene 8 pies de cuerda de evidencia y la corta en piezas de 1/3 de pie para etiquetarlas. ¿Qué significa 8 ÷ 1/3?
optional.explanationEs: Dividir entre 1/3 pregunta cuántas piezas de 1/3 de pie caben en 8 pies. Cada pie contiene 3 tercios, así que 8 × 3 = 24 piezas.
hints: Dividing by a fraction always asks the same question: how many pieces of that size fit inside the whole amount?
Name the two parts of the problem first — the whole amount of rope and the length of one piece. The whole amount comes first in the division.
Here the whole amount is 8 feet and each piece is 1/3 foot. Picture a single foot of rope: how many 1/3-foot pieces does one foot hold? Then extend that thinking to all 8 feet.
hintsEs: Dividir entre una fracción siempre hace la misma pregunta: ¿cuántas piezas de ese tamaño caben dentro de la cantidad total?
Primero nombra las dos partes del problema: la cantidad total de cuerda y el largo de una pieza. La cantidad total va primero en la división.
Aquí la cantidad total es 8 pies y cada pieza mide 1/3 de pie. Imagina un solo pie de cuerda: ¿cuántas piezas de 1/3 de pie caben en un pie? Luego extiende esa idea a los 8 pies.
choicesEs: Cuántas piezas de 1/3 de pie caben en 8 pies
8 piezas que miden 1/3 de pie cada una

optional.stem: Picture clue: a 5-inch fingerprint strip is split into 1/6-inch slivers under the microscope. Which division does the picture show, and what is the count?
optional.explanation: How many 1/6-inch slivers fit into 5 inches? Each inch holds 6 sixths, so 5 × 6 = 30 slivers.
choiceFeedback: You switched the numbers. Is the 5 the whole being split, or the size of each piece?
You flipped the division. The whole (5) should be first, and the piece size (1/6) should be second.
That's multiplication, not division. Count how many pieces fit, not the area they cover.
optional.stemEs: Pista visual: una tira de huella digital de 5 pulgadas se divide en tiritas de 1/6 de pulgada bajo el microscopio. ¿Qué división muestra la imagen y cuál es el conteo?
optional.explanationEs: ¿Cuántas tiritas de 1/6 de pulgada caben en 5 pulgadas? Cada pulgada contiene 6 sextos, así que 5 × 6 = 30 tiritas.
hints: The picture shows one long strip being cut into many small equal pieces, which is a division situation.
Write the whole length first, then divide by the size of one sliver. Cutting into smaller pieces makes the count larger than the length.
A single inch splits into 6 sixths. Use that to reason about how the count grows across all 5 inches.
hintsEs: La imagen muestra una tira larga cortada en muchas piezas iguales y pequeñas, lo cual es una situación de división.
Escribe primero el largo total y luego divide entre el tamaño de una tirita. Cortar en piezas más pequeñas hace que el conteo sea mayor que el largo.
Una sola pulgada se divide en 6 sextos. Usa eso para razonar cómo crece el conteo a lo largo de las 5 pulgadas.

optional.label: Match each detective story to the fraction-division expression and quotient that solves it.
optional.hint: Look at each story and ask: 'How many small pieces fit in a whole?' or 'What is each share?' That tells you the category.
optional.explanation: Every story cuts a whole amount into equal small pieces, so the total is the dividend and the piece size is the divisor: 9 ÷ 1/3 = 27 steps, 7 ÷ 1/4 = 28 zones, 10 ÷ 1/2 = 20 jars, 6 ÷ 1/6 = 36 samples, and 8 ÷ 1/5 = 40 clips. Notice the 6-foot wire cut into 1/6-foot samples still gives 36, not 1 — the denominator, not a match with the whole, is what multiplies.
optional.explanationEs: Cada historia corta una cantidad completa en piezas pequeñas iguales, así que el total es el dividendo y el tamaño de la pieza es el divisor: 9 ÷ 1/3 = 27 pasos, 7 ÷ 1/4 = 28 zonas, 10 ÷ 1/2 = 20 frascos, 6 ÷ 1/6 = 36 muestras y 8 ÷ 1/5 = 40 clips. Fíjate en que el cable de 6 pies cortado en muestras de 1/6 de pie da 36, no 1: lo que multiplica es el denominador, no que coincida con el entero.
optional.labelEs: Une cada historia del detective con la expresión de división de fracciones y el cociente que la resuelve.

optional.instructions: A detective must label each story: is the question asking 'how many groups (pieces)?' or 'how big is each share?'

categories.label: Asking: How Big Is Each Share?
categories.labelEs: Pregunta: ¿de qué tamaño es cada parte?

optional.hint: For each statement, think: does the divisor (the fraction we divide by) make the answer bigger or smaller than the original?
optional.explanation: The first three cards name a piece size — 1/4-foot pieces, 1/3-yard steps, 1/5-meter clips — and ask how many of those pieces fit, so they are "how many groups" questions. The last three name how many shares there are — 3 agents, 4 case files, 5 suspects — and ask how much each one gets, so they are "how big is each share" questions. Both are division; what changes is whether the divisor is a piece size or a number of shares.
optional.explanationEs: Las primeras tres tarjetas nombran un tamaño de pieza —piezas de 1/4 de pie, pasos de 1/3 de yarda, clips de 1/5 de metro— y preguntan cuántas de esas piezas caben, así que son preguntas de "cuántos grupos". Las últimas tres nombran cuántas partes hay —3 agentes, 4 expedientes, 5 sospechosos— y preguntan cuánto le toca a cada una, así que son preguntas de "qué tan grande es cada parte". Las dos son divisiones; lo que cambia es si el divisor es un tamaño de pieza o una cantidad de partes.
optional.instructionsEs: Un detective debe etiquetar cada historia: ¿la pregunta busca 'cuántos grupos (pedazos)?' o 'de qué tamaño es cada parte?'

workedExample.label: Case file
workedExample.work: A 9-foot strip of evidence tape is cut into 1/4-foot pieces. How many pieces?
workedExample.workEs: Una tira de cinta de evidencia de 9 pies se corta en piezas de 1/4 de pie. ¿Cuántas piezas salen?

workedExample.label: Detective writes
workedExample.work: This is 1/4 ÷ 9 — split the 1/4-foot piece among 9 sections.
workedExample.workEs: Esto es 1/4 ÷ 9 — repartir la pieza de 1/4 de pie entre 9 secciones.

optional.correctWork: The story asks 'how many 1/4-foot pieces fit into 9 feet,' so the dividend is the whole (9) and the divisor is the piece size (1/4): 9 ÷ 1/4. The detective swapped the dividend and divisor. The correct answer is 9 × 4 = 36 pieces.
hints: Which number is the whole amount being cut up, and which is the size of each small piece?
The dividend is the total you start with (9 feet); the divisor is the size of each piece (1/4 foot) — do not flip them.
optional.titleEs: Extensión de Nivel 2 — ¿Qué pregunta se está haciendo?
optional.explanation: The "Detective writes" step reverses the two numbers. The 9-foot strip is the total being cut, so it is the dividend, and 1/4 foot is the size of each piece, so it is the divisor: 9 ÷ 1/4. Each foot holds 4 quarter-foot pieces, so the answer is 9 × 4 = 36 pieces — an answer smaller than a single foot, like 1/36, cannot describe a count of pieces.
optional.explanationEs: El paso "Detective writes" invierte los dos números. La tira de 9 pies es el total que se corta, así que es el dividendo, y 1/4 de pie es el tamaño de cada pieza, así que es el divisor: 9 ÷ 1/4. Cada pie contiene 4 piezas de un cuarto de pie, así que la respuesta es 9 × 4 = 36 piezas; una respuesta menor que un solo pie, como 1/36, no puede describir una cantidad de piezas.
optional.correctWorkEs: La historia pregunta 'cuántas piezas de 1/4 de pie caben en 9 pies', así que el dividendo es el total (9) y el divisor es el tamaño de la pieza (1/4): 9 ÷ 1/4. El detective intercambió el dividendo y el divisor. La respuesta correcta es 9 × 4 = 36 piezas.
hintsEs: ¿Cuál número es la cantidad total que se está repartiendo y cuál es el tamaño de cada pedazo?
El dividendo es el total con el que empiezas (9 pies); el divisor es el tamaño de cada pedazo (1/4 de pie) — no los inviertas.

optional.stem: Model it: how many 1/4-size pieces fit inside 3/4?
optional.instructions: Build 3/4 on the top bar: set the bar to 4 equal parts and shade 3. Then build 1/4 on the comparison bar and confirm 3/4 > 1/4. Count how many 1/4-size pieces fit inside your shaded 3/4 — that count is exactly 3/4 ÷ 1/4.
optional.stemEs: Modélalo: ¿cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/4 caben dentro de 3/4?
optional.explanation: 3/4 ÷ 1/4 asks how many one-fourth pieces make up three-fourths. The fraction bar shows 3/4 already built out of fourth-size pieces, so counting those pieces gives the quotient: 3.
optional.explanationEs: 3/4 ÷ 1/4 pregunta cuántas piezas de un cuarto forman tres cuartos. La barra de fracciones muestra 3/4 construido con piezas del tamaño de un cuarto, así que contar esas piezas da el cociente: 3.
hints: Dividing by 1/4 asks how many fourth-size pieces fit inside the amount you have.
Build the amount on the bar using pieces that are each 1/4, then count pieces instead of calculating.
Shade 3/4 of the bar and mark it off in fourths. Each shaded section is one 1/4 piece — now count the shaded sections.
hintsEs: Dividir entre 1/4 pregunta cuántas piezas del tamaño de un cuarto caben en la cantidad que tienes.
Construye la cantidad en la barra usando piezas que midan 1/4 cada una y luego cuenta las piezas en lugar de calcular.
Sombrea 3/4 de la barra y márcala en cuartos. Cada sección sombreada es una pieza de 1/4 — ahora cuenta las secciones sombreadas.

approaching.explanation: 3 ÷ 1/4 asks: how many 1/4-size pieces fit into 3? The answer is 12, because each whole has 4 fourths, and 3 × 4 = 12.
choiceFeedback: That's multiplication (3 × 1/4). Division asks 'how many' pieces, not 'groups of' pieces.
Subtraction is not division. Division by a fraction asks 'how many pieces fit.'
That's finding a part of the whole. Division by a fraction asks 'how many of this size fit inside.'
hints: Re-read the expression: 3 is the total amount and 1/4 is the size of one piece. What question could that setup be asking?
Dividing by a fraction asks a counting question about pieces, not 'a part of.' Predict: should the result be bigger or smaller than 3?
Picture a 3-foot tape cut into 1/4-foot pieces. One whole foot already holds 4 of them — what question are you answering as you count?
approaching.explanationEs: 3 ÷ 1/4 pregunta: ¿cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/4 caben en 3? La respuesta es 12, porque cada entero tiene 4 cuartos, y 3 × 4 = 12.
choicesEs: Cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/4 caben en 3
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la expresión: 3 es la cantidad total y 1/4 es el tamaño de una pieza. ¿Qué pregunta podría estar haciendo ese planteamiento?
Dividir entre una fracción hace una pregunta de conteo sobre piezas, no de 'una parte de'. Predice: ¿el resultado debe ser mayor o menor que 3?
Imagina una cinta de 3 pies cortada en piezas de 1/4 de pie. Un pie entero ya tiene 4 de ellas: ¿qué pregunta respondes al contarlas?

approaching.stem: Which expression means 'how many 1/3-size pieces are in 2'?
approaching.explanation: Finding how many 1/3-size pieces fit into 2 is represented by 2 ÷ 1/3. The answer is 6.
choiceFeedback: That multiplies instead of divides. To find how many pieces fit, we divide by the piece size.
You flipped the order. The whole (2) goes first; the piece size (1/3) is the divisor.
Addition combines amounts. To find how many pieces fit, we divide.
hints: Find the two jobs: which number is the total being split, and which is the size of each piece?
Division setups read total ÷ piece size. The total always sits in front of the ÷ sign.
Here the total is 2 and each piece is 1/3. Build the expression with the total first, then check it against each choice.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué expresión significa "cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/3 hay en 2"?
approaching.explanationEs: Encontrar cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/3 caben en 2 se representa con 2 ÷ 1/3. La respuesta es 6.
hintsEs: Encuentra los dos papeles: ¿cuál número es el total que se reparte y cuál es el tamaño de cada pieza?
Los planteamientos de división se leen total ÷ tamaño de la pieza. El total siempre va delante del signo ÷.
Aquí el total es 2 y cada pieza es 1/3. Arma la expresión con el total primero y luego compárala con cada opción.

approaching.stem: A rope is 4 feet long. How many 1/2-foot pieces can be cut from it?
approaching.explanation: 4 ÷ 1/2 = 4 × 2 = 8 pieces. Each whole foot contains 2 halves, and 4 × 2 = 8.
choiceFeedback: You divided 4 by 2 (whole numbers). Remember: dividing by 1/2 means multiplying by 2 because two halves fit in each foot.
Dividing by 1/2 makes the answer bigger, not smaller. Each foot holds 2 halves.
You didn't multiply by the reciprocal. Dividing by 1/2 is like asking: how many halves in 4 wholes?
hints: Note the numbers: the rope is 4 feet long, and every piece is 1/2 foot — smaller than a whole foot.
Start small: figure out how many 1/2-foot pieces fit into just 1 foot of rope.
Each foot gives 2 half-foot pieces. Now count 2 pieces per foot, foot by foot, across the whole 4-foot rope.
approaching.stemEs: Una cuerda mide 4 pies de largo. ¿Cuántas piezas de 1/2 pie se pueden cortar de ella?
approaching.explanationEs: 4 ÷ 1/2 = 4 × 2 = 8 piezas. Cada pie entero contiene 2 mitades, y 4 × 2 = 8.
hintsEs: Fíjate en los números: la cuerda mide 4 pies y cada pieza mide 1/2 pie, menos que un pie entero.
Empieza en pequeño: averigua cuántas piezas de 1/2 pie caben en solo 1 pie de cuerda.
Cada pie da 2 piezas de medio pie. Ahora cuenta 2 piezas por pie, pie por pie, a lo largo de los 4 pies de cuerda.

approaching.stem: A half-pan of brownies is shared equally among 4 people. How much of the whole pan does each get?
approaching.explanation: This is 1/2 ÷ 4. Cutting the half into 4 equal parts makes eighths, so each person gets 1/8 of the whole pan.
choiceFeedback: That divides 4 by 1/2 — the opposite question.
That flips the problem into a multiplication of the wrong pair.
That gives the whole half to one person instead of sharing it.
hints: Draw half a pan, then split that half into 4 equal parts.
How many of those parts fit in the WHOLE pan?
Count how many of those equal parts it would take to cover the WHOLE pan — that number is the denominator.
approaching.stemEs: Medio molde de brownies se reparte en partes iguales entre 4 personas. ¿Cuánto del molde entero recibe cada una?
approaching.explanationEs: Esto es 1/2 ÷ 4. Cortar la mitad en 4 partes iguales forma octavos, así que cada persona recibe 1/8 del molde entero.
hintsEs: Dibuja medio molde y luego divide esa mitad en 4 partes iguales.
¿Cuántas de esas partes caben en TODO el molde?
Cuenta cuántas de esas partes iguales harían falta para cubrir TODO el molde — ese número es el denominador.

approaching.instructions: Sort each statement: does dividing by the fraction give a result GREATER than the dividend, or LESS than the dividend?
approaching.hint: Look at the problem. Is it asking 'how many equal shares' or 'how many pieces of this size fit inside'?
hints: Each card already shows the quotient and the dividend — like 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15. Compare those two numbers.
Check the divisor: dividing by a fraction under 1 makes the quotient grow; dividing by a whole number bigger than 1 shrinks it.
Try the first card: 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15. Ask 'is 15 more or less than the dividend 5?' and drag it to that side.
approaching.explanation: The three cards with unit-fraction divisors — 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15, 8 ÷ 1/2 = 16, and 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 — all land above their dividend, because pieces smaller than one whole means more of them fit. The three whole-number divisors — 4 ÷ 2 = 2, 10 ÷ 5 = 2, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 — land below, because splitting into groups larger than one gives each group less than the total. The size of the divisor compared to 1 is what decides the direction.
approaching.explanationEs: Las tres tarjetas con divisores de fracción unitaria —5 ÷ 1/3 = 15, 8 ÷ 1/2 = 16 y 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24— quedan por encima de su dividendo, porque si las piezas son más pequeñas que un entero, caben más. Los tres divisores que son números enteros —4 ÷ 2 = 2, 10 ÷ 5 = 2 y 12 ÷ 3 = 4— quedan por debajo, porque repartir en grupos mayores que uno le da a cada grupo menos que el total. El tamaño del divisor comparado con 1 es lo que decide la dirección.
approaching.instructionsEs: Clasifica cada afirmación: ¿dividir entre la fracción da un resultado MAYOR que el dividendo o MENOR que el dividendo?
hintsEs: Cada tarjeta ya muestra el cociente y el dividendo, como 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15. Compara esos dos números.
Revisa el divisor: dividir entre una fracción menor que 1 hace crecer el cociente; dividir entre un entero mayor que 1 lo achica.
Prueba la primera tarjeta: 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15. Pregunta '¿es 15 más o menos que el dividendo 5?' y arrástrala a ese lado.

approaching.explanation: 6 ÷ 1/5 means how many 1/5-size pieces fit into 6. Each whole has 5 fifths, so 6 × 5 = 30.
choiceFeedback: You multiplied 6 by 1/5 instead of dividing by 1/5. Dividing by a small fraction gives a much bigger answer.
You flipped it backward. Try: each whole has 5 fifths, so 6 wholes have 6 × 5 = 30 fifths.
Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 gives an answer bigger than you started with, not 1.
hints: 6 ÷ 1/5 asks: how many 1/5-size pieces fit into 6 wholes? Predict first — more or fewer than 6?
Find how many fifths make 1 whole, then use that count for all 6 wholes.
One whole holds 5 fifths. With 6 wholes, count 5 fifths for each whole — set up that multiplication.
approaching.explanationEs: 6 ÷ 1/5 significa cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/5 caben en 6. Cada entero tiene 5 quintos, así que 6 × 5 = 30.
hintsEs: 6 ÷ 1/5 pregunta: ¿cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/5 caben en 6 enteros? Predice primero: ¿más o menos de 6?
Averigua cuántos quintos forman 1 entero y luego usa esa cantidad para los 6 enteros.
Un entero tiene 5 quintos. Con 6 enteros, cuenta 5 quintos por cada entero y plantea esa multiplicación.

approaching.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: How many 1/3-foot pieces fit into 4 feet of tape? Find 4 ÷ 1/3.
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuántas piezas de 1/3 de pie caben en 4 pies de cinta? Encuentra 4 ÷ 1/3.

workedExample.label: Student writes
workedExample.work: Dividing makes the answer smaller, so 4 ÷ 1/3 = 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.3 pieces.
workedExample.workEs: Dividir hace la respuesta más pequeña, así que 4 ÷ 1/3 = 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.3 piezas.

approaching.correctWork: Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 makes the answer BIGGER, not smaller. Each whole foot holds 3 thirds, so 4 ÷ 1/3 = 4 × 3 = 12 pieces.
hints: How many 1/3-foot pieces fit inside just ONE foot?
If the pieces are smaller than a whole foot, will MORE or FEWER than 4 fit into 4 feet?
approaching.explanation: The "Student writes" step is wrong: it turns 4 ÷ 1/3 into 4 ÷ 3. Dividing by 1/3 asks how many 1/3-foot pieces fit into 4 feet, and each single foot already holds 3 of them, so 4 feet hold 4 × 3 = 12 pieces. Getting a result smaller than 4 should be an immediate signal that the divisor was replaced.
approaching.explanationEs: El paso "Student writes" está mal: convierte 4 ÷ 1/3 en 4 ÷ 3. Dividir entre 1/3 pregunta cuántas piezas de 1/3 de pie caben en 4 pies, y cada pie por sí solo ya contiene 3 de ellas, así que 4 pies contienen 4 × 3 = 12 piezas. Obtener un resultado menor que 4 debería avisarte de inmediato que se reemplazó el divisor.
approaching.correctWorkEs: Dividir entre una fracción menor que 1 hace la respuesta MÁS GRANDE, no más pequeña. Cada pie completo contiene 3 tercios, así que 4 ÷ 1/3 = 4 × 3 = 12 piezas.
hintsEs: ¿Cuántos pedazos de 1/3 de pie caben en UN solo pie?
Si los pedazos son menores que un pie entero, ¿cabrán MÁS o MENOS de 4 en 4 pies?

onLevel.label: Match each division expression to its quotient.
onLevel.hint: For each term on the left, write the division expression that matches the story. Then find the quotient.
hints: Every left card divides a whole number by a unit fraction — a 'how many pieces fit' question.
Shortcut: multiply the whole number by the bottom of the unit fraction (halves ×2, thirds ×3, and so on).
Start with 5 ÷ 1/2: each whole holds 2 halves, so count halves in 5 wholes and find that total on the right.
onLevel.explanation: Each card divides a whole number by a unit fraction, so count how many of that fraction fill one whole and repeat it: 5 ÷ 1/2 = 5 × 2 = 10, 6 ÷ 1/3 = 6 × 3 = 18, 2 ÷ 1/6 = 2 × 6 = 12, 4 ÷ 1/4 = 4 × 4 = 16, 3 ÷ 1/5 = 3 × 5 = 15, and 7 ÷ 1/2 = 7 × 2 = 14. Every quotient is larger than its dividend because the pieces being counted are smaller than one whole.
onLevel.explanationEs: Cada tarjeta divide un número entero entre una fracción unitaria, así que cuenta cuántas de esas fracciones llenan un entero y repítelo: 5 ÷ 1/2 = 5 × 2 = 10, 6 ÷ 1/3 = 6 × 3 = 18, 2 ÷ 1/6 = 2 × 6 = 12, 4 ÷ 1/4 = 4 × 4 = 16, 3 ÷ 1/5 = 3 × 5 = 15 y 7 ÷ 1/2 = 7 × 2 = 14. Cada cociente es mayor que su dividendo porque las piezas que se cuentan son más pequeñas que un entero.
onLevel.labelEs: Une cada expresión de división con su cociente.
hintsEs: Cada tarjeta de la izquierda divide un número entero entre una fracción unitaria: es una pregunta de 'cuántas piezas caben'.
Atajo: multiplica el número entero por el denominador de la fracción unitaria (medios ×2, tercios ×3, y así).
Empieza con 5 ÷ 1/2: cada entero tiene 2 medios, así que cuenta los medios en 5 enteros y busca ese total a la derecha.

onLevel.instructions: Use the bar model to count how many 1/6-size pieces fit into 3 wholes. All 3 wholes are shown, each split into sixths.
onLevel.label: Model 3 ÷ 1/6 with a bar model — all 3 wholes are shown, each split into sixths
onLevel.totalLabel: 3 wholes split into sixths — count all the 1/6 pieces
onLevel.questionText: How many 1/6-size pieces fit into 3 wholes?
onLevel.hint: Count how many sections of size 1/6 fit into each whole on the bar. Then add them all up.
hints: Look at the bar: all 3 wholes are already split into 1/6-size sections, marked whole 1, whole 2, whole 3.
Count how many sixths fill just one whole first, then use that count for all three wholes.
One whole holds 6 sixths. Keep counting past 6 as you move through whole 2 and whole 3.
onLevel.explanation: Whole 1 is made of 6 sixths, and whole 2 and whole 3 are each made of 6 more, so the bar shows 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 pieces of size 1/6. That is exactly what 3 ÷ 1/6 asks: how many 1/6-size pieces fit into 3 wholes. The answer is 18.
onLevel.explanationEs: El entero 1 está formado por 6 sextos, y el entero 2 y el entero 3 tienen 6 cada uno, así que el modelo muestra 6 + 6 + 6 = 18 piezas de tamaño 1/6. Eso es exactamente lo que pregunta 3 ÷ 1/6: cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/6 caben en 3 enteros. La respuesta es 18.
hintsEs: Mira la barra: los 3 enteros ya están divididos en secciones de tamaño 1/6, marcadas entero 1, entero 2 y entero 3.
Cuenta primero cuántos sextos llenan un solo entero y luego usa ese conteo para los tres enteros.
Un entero contiene 6 sextos. Sigue contando más allá de 6 al pasar por el entero 2 y el entero 3.

onLevel.instructions: Plot the quotient of each expression on the number line.
onLevel.label: Place each result on the number line
onLevel.hint: Calculate each quotient first. Then plot the answer on the number line at the correct tick mark.
hints: Each label shows its quotient after the equals sign — like 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12.
The line runs 0 to 24 with ticks every 2. Match each quotient to its tick.
Start with 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12: count ticks by 2s from 0 (2, 4, 6, …) and drop the point on 12.
onLevel.explanation: Work out each quotient before plotting: 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12, 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20, and 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6. Because the line runs from 0 to 24 with a tick every 2, all three answers land exactly on ticks — 12 is halfway across, 20 is two ticks before 24, and 6 is the third tick from 0.
onLevel.explanationEs: Calcula cada cociente antes de marcarlo: 3 ÷ 1/4 = 12, 4 ÷ 1/5 = 20 y 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6. Como la recta va de 0 a 24 con una marca cada 2, las tres respuestas caen exactamente en marcas: 12 está a la mitad, 20 está dos marcas antes de 24 y 6 es la tercera marca desde 0.

onLevel.stem: A shelf is 5 feet long. Books are each 1/4 foot wide. How many books fit on the shelf? Which expression represents this?
onLevel.explanation: You are finding how many 1/4-foot pieces fit into 5 feet, which is 5 ÷ 1/4 = 5 × 4 = 20 books.
choiceFeedback: That multiplies instead of dividing. To count pieces that fit, divide the whole by the piece size.
You flipped the division. The shelf length (5) is the dividend; the book width (1/4) is the divisor.
Addition combines lengths. To find how many books fit, divide the shelf length by one book's width.
hints: Spot the roles: 5 feet is the whole shelf, and 1/4 foot is the width of one book.
Counting how many books fit means total ÷ piece size — and the count should be bigger than 5, since books are thin.
Each 1 foot of shelf fits 4 books. Use that to test which setup gives a count that matches all 5 feet.
onLevel.stemEs: Un estante mide 5 pies de largo. Cada libro tiene 1/4 de pie de ancho. ¿Cuántos libros caben en el estante? ¿Qué expresión representa esto?
onLevel.explanationEs: Estás buscando cuántas piezas de 1/4 de pie caben en 5 pies, que es 5 ÷ 1/4 = 5 × 4 = 20 libros.
hintsEs: Identifica los papeles: 5 pies es el estante completo y 1/4 de pie es el ancho de un libro.
Contar cuántos libros caben significa total ÷ tamaño de la pieza, y el conteo debe ser mayor que 5 porque los libros son delgados.
Cada pie de estante cabe 4 libros. Úsalo para probar qué planteamiento da un conteo que cubra los 5 pies.

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Problem
workedExample.work: How many 1/5-cup scoops fill a 6-cup container? Find 6 ÷ 1/5.
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuántas medidas de 1/5 de taza llenan un recipiente de 6 tazas? Encuentra 6 ÷ 1/5.

workedExample.label: Student writes
workedExample.work: I will flip the first number instead of the divisor: 6 ÷ 1/5 = 1/6 × 5 = 5/6 scoop.
workedExample.workEs: Voy a voltear el primer número en lugar del divisor: 6 ÷ 1/5 = 1/6 × 5 = 5/6 de medida.

onLevel.correctWork: To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the DIVISOR (1/5), not the dividend. The reciprocal of 1/5 is 5, so 6 ÷ 1/5 = 6 × 5 = 30 scoops.
hints: Which number do you flip when you divide — the dividend (6) or the divisor (1/5)?
How many 1/5-cup scoops fit in just ONE cup? Then there are 6 cups.
onLevel.explanation: In the "Student writes" step the reciprocal was taken of the dividend 6 instead of the divisor 1/5. Only the divisor gets flipped: the reciprocal of 1/5 is 5, so 6 ÷ 1/5 = 6 × 5 = 30 scoops. That matches the story too — each cup holds 5 one-fifth scoops, and there are 6 cups.
onLevel.explanationEs: En el paso "Student writes" se tomó el recíproco del dividendo 6 en lugar del divisor 1/5. Solo se invierte el divisor: el recíproco de 1/5 es 5, así que 6 ÷ 1/5 = 6 × 5 = 30 cucharadas. Eso también coincide con la historia: cada taza contiene 5 cucharadas de un quinto, y hay 6 tazas.
onLevel.correctWorkEs: Para dividir, multiplica por el recíproco del DIVISOR (1/5), no del dividendo. El recíproco de 1/5 es 5, así que 6 ÷ 1/5 = 6 × 5 = 30 medidas.
hintsEs: ¿Cuál número volteas al dividir — el dividendo (6) o el divisor (1/5)?
¿Cuántas medidas de 1/5 de taza caben en UNA sola taza? Luego hay 6 tazas.

extending.title: Find the Interpretation Error
extending.correctWork: 4 ÷ 1/5 means 'how many 1/5-size pieces fit into 4,' not '1/5 of 4.' The correct answer is 4 × 5 = 20.
hints: Does dividing by 1/5 make the result smaller or larger than 4?
The student confused 'divide by 1/5' with 'multiply by 1/5.' What is the difference?
extending.explanation: The "Student says" step rewrites division as multiplication: "1/5 of 4" means 1/5 × 4, which is a different question. 4 ÷ 1/5 asks how many 1/5-size pieces fit inside 4, and each whole holds 5 of them, so the quotient is 4 × 5 = 20. The answer 4/5 is smaller than the dividend, which cannot happen when you divide by a number less than 1.
extending.explanationEs: El paso "Student says" convierte la división en multiplicación: "1/5 de 4" significa 1/5 × 4, que es otra pregunta. 4 ÷ 1/5 pregunta cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/5 caben dentro de 4, y cada entero contiene 5 de ellas, así que el cociente es 4 × 5 = 20. La respuesta 4/5 es menor que el dividendo, y eso no puede pasar cuando divides entre un número menor que 1.
extending.correctWorkEs: 4 ÷ 1/5 significa 'cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/5 caben en 4', no '1/5 de 4'. La respuesta correcta es 4 × 5 = 20.
hintsEs: ¿Dividir entre 1/5 hace el resultado menor o mayor que 4?
El estudiante confundió 'dividir entre 1/5' con 'multiplicar por 1/5'. ¿Cuál es la diferencia?

extending.prompt: Dividing 6 by 1/2 gives 12, but dividing 6 by 2 gives 3. How can dividing by a smaller number (1/2) give a bigger answer than dividing by a larger number (2)? Explain using a real-world example.
extending.sentenceFrame: When I divide 6 by 2, I am ___. When I divide 6 by 1/2, I am ___. The answer is bigger because ___.
extending.hint: Compare the two divisions: what question does each one ask? Use 'fit into' and 'share' in your thinking.
hints: Re-read both: 6 ÷ 2 splits 6 into 2 equal groups, but 6 ÷ 1/2 counts how many half-size pieces fit into 6.
Pick a real object — 6 sandwiches shared between 2 people versus 6 sandwiches cut into halves — and describe both.
Start your answer with the sharing story (6 split into 2 groups), then explain what cutting into halves does to the count.
extending.explanation: The two expressions ask different questions. 6 ÷ 2 shares 6 into 2 equal groups, so each group gets 3. 6 ÷ 1/2 counts how many half-size pieces fit inside 6, and since each whole holds 2 halves, there are 12. Smaller pieces means a bigger count, so dividing by 1/2 gives a larger quotient than dividing by 2.
extending.explanationEs: Las dos expresiones hacen preguntas distintas. 6 ÷ 2 reparte 6 en 2 grupos iguales, así que a cada grupo le tocan 3. 6 ÷ 1/2 cuenta cuántas piezas de medio caben dentro de 6 y, como cada entero contiene 2 mitades, hay 12. Piezas más pequeñas significan una cuenta más grande, así que dividir entre 1/2 da un cociente mayor que dividir entre 2.
extending.promptEs: Dividir 6 entre 1/2 da 12, pero dividir 6 entre 2 da 3. ¿Cómo puede dividir entre un número más pequeño (1/2) dar una respuesta más grande que dividir entre un número más grande (2)? Explica con un ejemplo de la vida real.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer ambas: 6 ÷ 2 reparte 6 en 2 grupos iguales, pero 6 ÷ 1/2 cuenta cuántas piezas de medio tamaño caben en 6.
Escoge un objeto real —6 sándwiches repartidos entre 2 personas frente a 6 sándwiches cortados por la mitad— y describe las dos situaciones.
Empieza tu respuesta con la historia de repartir (6 en 2 grupos) y luego explica qué le hace al conteo cortar por la mitad.

extending.label: Complete the pattern: as the unit fraction divisor gets smaller, what happens to the quotient?
extending.hint: For each row, think about what happens to the quotient as the divisor gets smaller. Look for the pattern.
hints: Every row divides the same 2 by a smaller and smaller unit fraction — watch what the quotient does.
For each row, count how many of that fraction fit in 1 whole, then double it because the dividend is 2.
First row: 2 ÷ 1/2 — one whole holds 2 halves, so count the halves in two wholes. Then compare with the next row's quotient.
extending.explanation: The dividend stays at 2 while the divisor shrinks, so the quotients climb: 2 ÷ 1/2 = 4, 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6, 2 ÷ 1/4 = 8, 2 ÷ 1/6 = 12, and 2 ÷ 1/10 = 20. Each quotient is 2 times the denominator, because that denominator tells you how many pieces fit in one whole. The pattern column names the rule: a smaller divisor produces a larger quotient.
extending.explanationEs: El dividendo se queda en 2 mientras el divisor se hace más pequeño, así que los cocientes suben: 2 ÷ 1/2 = 4, 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6, 2 ÷ 1/4 = 8, 2 ÷ 1/6 = 12 y 2 ÷ 1/10 = 20. Cada cociente es 2 veces el denominador, porque ese denominador te dice cuántas piezas caben en un entero. La columna del patrón nombra la regla: un divisor más pequeño produce un cociente más grande.
extending.labelEs: Completa el patrón: a medida que el divisor de fracción unitaria se hace más pequeño, ¿qué le pasa al cociente?
hintsEs: Cada fila divide el mismo 2 entre una fracción unitaria cada vez más pequeña: observa qué le pasa al cociente.
Para cada fila, cuenta cuántas de esa fracción caben en 1 entero y luego duplícalo porque el dividendo es 2.
Primera fila: 2 ÷ 1/2 — un entero tiene 2 medios, así que cuenta los medios en dos enteros. Después compara con el cociente de la fila siguiente.

optionalActivity.name: Fraction Division Story Match
optionalActivity.intro: Crack the case file: match each detective situation to the fraction-division expression and picture that solves it.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Interpret Division of Fractions is assuming that dividing always makes the answer smaller. For 4 ÷ 1/3, students reason 'dividing shrinks the number' and compute 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 1.3 instead of asking how many 1/3-foot pieces fit into 4 feet (each whole foot holds 3 thirds, so 4 × 3 = 12). Before you submit, check: if the divisor is a fraction smaller than 1, the quotient must be BIGGER than the dividend, not smaller.

diagram.title: 6 Yards of Tape in Thirds
diagram.caption: Each yard splits into three 1/3-yard sections; count all the parts to see that 6 ÷ 1/3 = 18 sections fit into the 6-yard tape.

connect.scenario: A detective has 6 yards of crime scene tape. She needs to mark off sections that are each 1/3 of a yard. She wants to know how many sections she can mark.
connect.promptQuestion: How does interpreting fraction division help the detective?
connect.prompt: The detective can mark ___ sections because 6 ÷ 1/3 = ___.

check.explanation: Ask how many 1/3-yard pieces fit in 6 yards. Each yard holds 3 of them, and 6 × 3 = 18.

check.stem: Why is the answer bigger than 6?
choices: Because the pieces are smaller than a whole yard, so many of them fit
Because dividing always makes numbers bigger
check.explanation: Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a larger result: each piece is smaller than one yard, so more pieces fit.

check.stem: If each section were 1/2 yard instead, how many sections?
check.explanation: 6 ÷ 1/2 = 12. Bigger pieces means fewer of them fit.

connect.modelAnswer: 6 ÷ 1/3 = 18 sections. Each yard of tape splits into three 1/3-yard sections, and 6 × 3 = 18. Dividing by a fraction less than 1 always gives an answer larger than the amount you started with.

exitTicket.stem: What does 5 ÷ 1/4 mean, and what is the quotient?
choices: How many 1/4-size pieces fit into 5; quotient is 20
exitTicket.explanation: 5 ÷ 1/4 means 'how many 1/4-size pieces fit into 5.' Since each whole has 4 fourths, 5 × 4 = 20.
choiceFeedback: That's multiplication. Does 5 groups of 1/4 describe 'dividing' or 'multiplying'?
Taking 1/4 of 5 is multiplication. Division by a fraction asks 'how many pieces fit inside.'
Subtraction is not the operation here. Division by 1/4 asks how many of those small pieces fit.
hints: Re-read 5 ÷ 1/4: is 5 the total being cut up, or the size of one piece?
Dividing by a fraction under 1 asks how many pieces fit — so predict whether the quotient beats 5 before checking choices.
One whole holds 4 fourths. Count fourths across all 5 wholes, then match both the meaning and your count to a choice.

printables.name: Fraction Division Model Match
printables.desc: Students match fraction-division situations to equations and quotients, then explain what each quotient means.

printables.name: Interpret Division of Fractions — Color by Number
printables.desc: Solve each problem, then color by the answer to reveal a picture.

graphicNovel.title: Master Chef Kitchen — Recipe Rescue (Part 1)
graphicNovel.desc: Interactive graphic novel — making sense of what dividing by a fraction means, to rescue the recipe. Read straight through; gates coach but never block. Not graded.

mission.title: The Fraction Vault
mission.story: You are the lead forensic analyst at the Reyes Detective Agency. A 3-foot strip of evidence tape must be cut into exact 1/4-foot sections before it can be logged — and the vault that holds the case file only opens once you know how many pieces that makes. Interpret fraction division and crack the case.
mission.objective: Interpret division by a unit fraction as 'how many pieces fit' so you can log the evidence correctly.

scenes.name: Crime Scene
scenes.text: Examine the 3-foot tape that must be cut into 1/4-foot evidence sections.

scenes.name: Case Notes
scenes.text: Log the key terms: dividend, divisor, quotient, reciprocal, and unit fraction.

scenes.name: Evidence Bench
scenes.text: Partition a bar into fourths to see exactly how many 1/4-pieces fit into a whole.

scenes.name: Lab Analysis
scenes.text: Run the analysis problems. The lab adapts the difficulty to keep you in the zone.

scenes.name: Field Work
scenes.text: Apply fraction division to mark off real crime-scene tape sections.

scenes.name: Case Closed
scenes.text: File your report and prove you can interpret fraction division.

simulation.instructions: Partition the bar into 4 equal parts to model one whole foot of evidence tape. Each shaded part is one 1/4-foot section — see how the unit fraction tiles the whole.

finale.title: Case Closed!
finale.text: Twelve evidence sections logged perfectly, and the vault swung open. The Reyes Detective Agency cracked its biggest case — because you knew exactly how to interpret 3 ÷ 1/4.

items.meaning: Finding how many groups of one fraction fit inside another amount
The number you are splitting up in a division problem
The number you split by in a division problem

steps: 1. Whole divided by unit fraction: How many fraction pieces fit into the whole (result is larger)
2. Unit fraction divided by whole: Split the fraction piece into smaller parts (result is smaller)
3. Multiply by the denominator of the unit fraction
